course.title: AP U.S. History
course.description: Trace how Americans have argued over identity, power, work, and their place in the world, from the societies that existed before 1491 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Follow the nation's development from early contact and colonization through independence, civil war, industrialization, world wars, and recent decades.

unit.title: Period 4
unit.description: Follow the rise of party politics and a more participatory democracy, the market revolution, westward expansion and foreign policy, the Second Great Awakening and reform, and the growth of slavery from 1800 to 1848.

firstTopic.title: Contextualizing Period 4
firstTopic.summary: The context for Period 4: a more participatory democracy and a new national culture, an economy transformed by innovation, and a nation that expanded westward and argued over slavery, 1800–1848.

framework.name: Course themes
framework.title: Use the course themes to choose your evidence
framework.intro: The themes connect developments across all nine periods. A piece of evidence can fit more than one theme; choose the one that answers the prompt.
framework.sourceNote: Theme names, codes, and descriptions follow the AP U.S. History Course and Exam Description (fall 2026).

themes.title: American and National Identity
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why definitions of American and national identity and values have developed among the diverse and changing population of North America as well as on related topics, such as citizenship, constitutionalism, foreign policy, assimilation, and American exceptionalism.
themes.question: Who counted as American, and what did people believe the nation stood for?
themes.example: Debates over ratifying the Constitution turned on what kind of republic Americans wanted.

themes.title: Work, Exchange, and Technology
themes.description: This theme focuses on the factors behind the development of systems of economic exchange, particularly the role of technology, economic markets, and government.
themes.question: How did people earn a living, trade, and use new technology?
themes.example: Canals and railroads tied farmers in the West to markets in the East.

themes.title: Geography and the Environment
themes.description: This theme focuses on the role of geography and both the natural and human-made environments in the social and political developments in what would become the United States.
themes.question: How did land, climate, and resources shape choices, and how did people change them?
themes.example: The Chesapeake's climate suited tobacco, which shaped its labor system.

themes.title: Migration and Settlement
themes.description: This theme focuses on why and how the various people who moved to and within the United States both adapted to and transformed their new social and physical environments.
themes.question: Why did people move, and how did they change the places they settled?
themes.example: The Great Migration brought African Americans from the rural South to northern cities.

themes.title: Politics and Power
themes.description: This theme focuses on how different social and political groups have influenced society and government in the United States as well as how political beliefs and institutions have changed over time.
themes.question: Who held power, how did they use it, and who challenged it?
themes.example: The New Deal expanded the federal government's role in the economy.

themes.title: America in the World
themes.description: This theme focuses on the interactions between nations that affected North American history in the colonial period and on the influence of the United States on world affairs.
themes.question: How did contact, trade, diplomacy, and war connect America to other nations?
themes.example: The Seven Years' War left Britain in debt and changed its policies toward the colonies.

themes.title: American and Regional Culture
themes.description: This theme focuses on the how and why national, regional, and group cultures developed and changed as well as how culture has shaped government policy and the economy.
themes.question: How did beliefs, religion, arts, and media develop and shape public life?
themes.example: The Second Great Awakening inspired many Americans to join reform movements.

themes.title: Social Structures
themes.description: This theme focuses on how and why systems of social organization develop and change as well as the impact that these systems have on the broader society.
themes.question: How were people ranked by race, class, and gender, and how did that change?
themes.example: The growth of a middle class in the Gilded Age changed ideas about leisure and family.

lesson.title: The Society of the South in the Early Republic
lesson.summary: How cotton, soil exhaustion, and the westward movement of slavery shaped the South's economy, society, and sense of regional identity from 1800 to 1848.
learningGoals: Explain how reliance on agricultural staples shaped a distinctive Southern identity.
Explain how overcultivation and the search for fertile land moved slavery west.
Explain how Southern leaders defended slavery as part of the Southern way of life.
lesson.bigIdea: The South tied its economy to cotton and slavery, expanded slavery into new lands as old fields wore out, and developed a regional identity that its leaders defended.
lesson.context: The CED asks you to explain how geographic and environmental factors shaped the development of the South. Link soil, climate, and rivers to crops, labor, migration, and the South's political and cultural defense of slavery.

sections.title: Cotton and Southern identity

blocks.text: Southern business leaders continued to rely on the production and export of traditional agricultural staples, contributing to the growth of a distinctive Southern regional identity. Cotton became the leading crop after the invention of the cotton gin in 1793 and the demand of British and New England textile mills. By the 1830s and 1840s cotton made up roughly half of the nation's exports by value, and the South's long growing season and warm, wet climate suited it well.

While the North built factories, canals, and railroads, the South invested its wealth in land and in enslaved laborers. It had fewer cities, banks, and factories, and fewer immigrants, than the North. Its economy relied on exports and on Northern and British merchants and bankers, and these differences encouraged white Southerners to see their region as distinct.

sections.takeaway: Dependence on cotton and slave labor set the South apart from the North and shaped its regional identity.

sections.title: Overcultivation and the westward movement of slavery
sections.conceptTitle: Overcultivation and the westward movement of slavery

blocks.text: As overcultivation depleted arable land in the Southeast, slaveholders began relocating their plantations to more fertile lands west of the Appalachians, where the institution of slavery continued to grow. Tobacco and cotton had worn out the soil of Virginia, the Carolinas, and Georgia. Planters moved to Alabama, Mississippi, Louisiana, and later Texas, where the black soil of the Mississippi Valley and the Gulf plains was rich.

The movement was also a forced migration of enslaved people. Between 1790 and 1860 about a million enslaved people were moved from the Upper South to the Deep South, many by traders who sold them in markets such as Richmond and New Orleans, which broke up families. This westward expansion of slavery caused the contests over new territories discussed in Topic 4.3.

sections.takeaway: Soil exhaustion pushed planters west, and enslaved people were moved by force to new cotton lands.

sections.title: Slavery as a Southern way of life
sections.conceptTitle: Slavery as a Southern way of life

blocks.text: In the South, although the majority of Southerners owned no enslaved persons, most leaders argued that slavery was part of the Southern way of life. About three-fourths of white Southern families owned no enslaved people, and many were yeoman farmers who grew food and some cotton on small farms. A small group of large planters held most of the enslaved people, most of the wealth, and most of the political power.

After the 1830s, as abolitionism grew in the North, many Southern leaders stopped calling slavery a necessary evil and began to defend it as a “positive good.” John C. Calhoun and others argued that slavery benefited both enslaved and enslavers. Proslavery writers used economics, religion, and claims about race to support their case. White Southerners who did not own slaves often supported slavery because they hoped to own slaves someday and because it gave them a claim to higher status than Black people.

blocks.title: Common trap
blocks.text: Do not assume that most white Southerners owned enslaved people. Most owned none, but the large planters who did dominated Southern politics and economic life.

sections.takeaway: Planters led the South, and as abolitionism grew, Southern leaders defended slavery as a positive good and as part of their way of life.

connections.title: Pulling Period 4 together
connections.body: The South's development, the market revolution, and westward expansion all shaped American identity. Topic 4.14 asks how to reason about causes across the period.
connections.transferQuestion: How did the demand of Northern and British textile mills affect Southern society?
connections.feedback: A strong answer notes that demand for cotton raised the value of land and enslaved labor, tied the South to export markets, and expanded slavery to new lands.
